name: Mahāpurāṇas
summary: The conventional set of eighteen 'great' Purāṇas. The tradition agrees on the number eighteen but not on the membership: lists such as Viṣṇu Purāṇa 3.6 and Bhāgavata 12.7 name a Śaiva Purāṇa where the Matsya and Nārada lists name the Vāyu (the Kūrma names both).
details:
The constituted text of the Viṣṇu Purāṇa critical edition (Pathak) lists eighteen purāṇas at 3.6.21–23 (Brāhma, Pādma, Vaiṣṇava, Śaiva, Bhāgavata, Nāradīya, Mārkaṇḍeya, Āgneya, Bhaviṣya, Brahmavaivarta, Laiṅga, Vārāha, Skānda, Vāmana, Kaurma, Mātsya, Gāruḍa, Brahmāṇḍa); the half-line naming them 'mahāpurāṇas' and adding 'upapurāṇas' is printed as an insertion (3.6.23*8). Rocher notes that the term mahāpurāṇa is rare and probably late.

Lists differ in the fourth place: Śaiva (ViP 3.6.21; BhP 12.7.23; Liṅga 1.39.61; Śiva P 7.1.1.43) versus Vāyavīya (Matsya 53.18; Nārada 1.92.26); the Kūrma (1.1.13–15) keeps Śaiva fourth and adds a Vāyavīya near the end. The Bhāgavata (12.13.4–9) assigns verse counts totalling 400,000. A later classification (Padma Purāṇa, recall) sorts the eighteen into sāttvika, rājasa and tāmasa groups; Matsya 53.68–69 already links sāttvika Purāṇas with Hari, rājasa with Brahmā and tāmasa with Agni and Śiva.

name: Upapurāṇas
summary: 'Secondary' Purāṇas, also conventionally eighteen, whose lists disagree even more than those of the Mahāpurāṇas; several (Viṣṇudharmottara, Kālikā, Narasiṃha, Devī Bhāgavata in some lists) are as old or as influential as Mahāpurāṇas.
details: Matsya Purāṇa 53.60–63 already names 'subdivisions' (upabheda): a Nārasiṃha of 18,000 verses, a Nandī, a Sāmba and an Āditya Purāṇa. Hazra characterised the distinction as one of renown (a well-known Purāṇa is 'mahā', a lesser-known one 'upa'); Rocher regards the distinction as ahistorical.

name: Dharmaśāstra
summary: The Sanskrit genre of normative treatises on dharma (Manu, Yājñavalkya, Nārada, Viṣṇu and others), together with their commentaries and digests; included here because Manusmṛti 1 supplies one of the earliest yuga reckonings.

name: Viṣṇu Purāṇa
summary: A Vaiṣṇava Mahāpurāṇa of six books (aṃśas), narrated by Parāśara to Maitreya, often taken as the Purāṇa that best preserves the five 'marks' (pañcalakṣaṇa); book 5 is a sustained life of Kṛṣṇa.
details:
Book 1: creation, Varāha (1.4), time units and yugas (1.3), the churning of the ocean (1.9), Dhruva (1.11–12), Prahlāda (1.16–20). Book 2: cosmography. Book 3: manvantaras (3.1–2), Vyāsa and the Veda, the list of eighteen purāṇas and the five marks (3.6). Book 4: royal genealogies of the Solar and Lunar lines and the prophetic dynasties of the Kali age down to the Guptas (4.24). Book 5: Kṛṣṇa. Book 6: dissolution and liberation.

A critical edition (M. M. Pathak, Oriental Institute Vadodara 1997–99) exists; its apparatus relegates some well-known lines to insertions, including the half-verse that calls the eighteen 'mahāpurāṇas' (3.6.23*8).

Rocher (1986) stresses that no Purāṇa can be dated as a whole: each is a layered, 'fluid' text transmitted in divergent manuscript versions, so any date applies only to a layer, a recension or a datable reference.

name: Bhāgavata Purāṇa
summary: The most influential Vaiṣṇava Purāṇa, in twelve books (skandhas), narrated by Śuka to King Parīkṣit; its tenth book on Kṛṣṇa's life became a foundation of later Kṛṣṇa devotion, and 1.3.28 declares Kṛṣṇa 'Bhagavān himself'.
details:
Key loci verified in the GRETIL e-text: the 22 avatāras (1.3.6–25) and the declaration 'ete cāṃśakalāḥ puṃsaḥ kṛṣṇas tu bhagavān svayam' (1.3.28); a second, longer avatāra catalogue (2.7.1–38); time and yugas (3.11.18–24); Dhruva (4.8–12); Prahlāda and Narasiṃha (7.1–10, the pillar 7.8.17–19); Gajendra (8.2–4); the churning (8.5–12, Śiva drinks the hālāhala 8.7.43); the current manvantara (8.13.1–6); Vāmana and Bali (8.15–23); Matsya and Satyavrata (8.24); dynasties (9); Kṛṣṇa (10); ten lakṣaṇas of a Purāṇa (12.7.9–10, noting that some count five) and the list of eighteen (12.7.23–24); verse counts (12.13.4–9).

Dating is contested: many scholars, following Hardy's arguments for South Indian (Āḻvār-influenced) composition, place the final redaction in the 9th–early 10th century; others argue for a substantially earlier (Gupta-period) text. van Buitenen drew attention to its deliberately Vedic, archaising language. Rocher (1986) stresses that no Purāṇa can be dated as a whole: each is a layered, 'fluid' text transmitted in divergent manuscript versions, so any date applies only to a layer, a recension or a datable reference.

name: Śiva Purāṇa
subtype: Mahāpurāṇa (contested; some lists give the Vāyu instead)
summary: A large Śaiva compilation organised in saṃhitās (seven in the common Bombay text: Vidyeśvara, Rudra, Śatarudra, Koṭirudra, Umā, Kailāsa, Vāyavīya) that narrates Śiva's manifestations, the Liṅgodbhava and Śaiva ritual.
details:
The text describes itself as an abridgement (24,000 verses, seven saṃhitās) of a 100,000-verse Śaiva Purāṇa of twelve saṃhitās (ŚivP 1.2.49–61, 7.1.1.49–60). Its Vidyeśvara-saṃhitā (1.5–9) tells the Liṅgodbhava with the distinctive episode of the ketakī flower as Brahmā's false witness (1.7.19–27).

Whether the 'Śaiva' of the eighteen-lists is this text or the Vāyu Purāṇa was debated in the 19th–20th centuries; modern scholarship treats them as different works. Rocher (1986) stresses that no Purāṇa can be dated as a whole: each is a layered, 'fluid' text transmitted in divergent manuscript versions, so any date applies only to a layer, a recension or a datable reference.

name: Vāyu Purāṇa
summary: One of the oldest Purāṇas, Śaiva in orientation and closely parallel to the Brahmāṇḍa (the two are thought to derive from one original); the Mahābhārata (CE 3.189.14) already refers to a purāṇa 'proclaimed by Vāyu'.
details:
Matsya 53.18 describes the Vāyavīya as taught by Vāyu in connection with the Śveta-kalpa and 'joined with the greatness of Rudra', 24,000 verses — the same count the Bhāgavata gives for the 'Śaiva'. It occupies the fourth place in the Matsya and Nārada lists; the Kūrma names it after the Gāruḍa, possibly equating it with the Brahmāṇḍa.

With the Brahmāṇḍa and Matsya it is a principal witness for the Kali-age dynastic lists studied by Pargiter (1913). Its Gayā-māhātmya is a later addition (Hazra). Rocher (1986) stresses that no Purāṇa can be dated as a whole: each is a layered, 'fluid' text transmitted in divergent manuscript versions, so any date applies only to a layer, a recension or a datable reference.

name: Skanda Purāṇa
summary: The largest Purāṇa by reputation (81,100 verses per BhP 12.13.7), known in print as a vast compendium of khaṇḍas (Māheśvara, Vaiṣṇava, Brahma, Kāśī, Avantī, Nāgara, Prabhāsa) rich in tīrtha-māhātmyas; scholars distinguish it from the much earlier 'original' Skandapurāṇa preserved in Nepalese manuscripts.
details:
The printed khaṇḍas came into existence in many cases after the 12th century (the Kāśī-khaṇḍa reached its present form around the 13th–14th century); they serve as the principal sthala-purāṇic charters of north and west Indian pilgrimage. The edited early text (text:skandapurana-early) is a different, coherent work of the late 6th–early 7th century, sharing mainly the name.

Rocher (1986) stresses that no Purāṇa can be dated as a whole: each is a layered, 'fluid' text transmitted in divergent manuscript versions, so any date applies only to a layer, a recension or a datable reference.

name: Skandapurāṇa (early recension, Nepalese manuscripts)
summary: The 'original' Skandapurāṇa, a Pāśupata-milieu Śaiva Purāṇa composed probably in the late 6th or early 7th century (perhaps at Vārāṇasī) and transmitted in Nepalese palm-leaf manuscripts, one of which, dated 810 CE, is the oldest dated Purāṇa manuscript known; it is being critically edited by the Groningen–Leiden Skandapurāṇa project.
details:
The edition (vol. I 1998, Adriaensen–Bakker–Isaacson; later vols. by Bakker, Bisschop, Yokochi) shows a text centred on Śiva's family — the birth of Skanda, Pārvatī's asceticism, Andhaka — and on Śaiva holy places, with a strongly Pāśupata outlook. Bakker has proposed that it was conceived in Maukhari times and completed in the reign of Harṣa; the manuscripts S1 (dated 810 CE) and others are held in Kathmandu.

The ambiguity of the era used in the colophon leaves a small uncertainty (810/811 CE).

name: Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa
summary: A comparatively non-sectarian and probably early Mahāpurāṇa narrated by the sage Mārkaṇḍeya to the wise birds; it contains the Devī Māhātmya (chapters 81–93 in the common text).
details:
Its frame (birds who heard the Mahābhārata) and its accounts of Hariścandra, Madālasā and the manvantaras make it one of the most varied Purāṇas. The Devī Māhātmya is set in the Sāvarṇika manvantara (colophons of MkP 81–93). A Nepalese palm-leaf manuscript dated 998 CE is reported in the secondary literature (not verified here).

Rocher (1986) stresses that no Purāṇa can be dated as a whole: each is a layered, 'fluid' text transmitted in divergent manuscript versions, so any date applies only to a layer, a recension or a datable reference.

name: Devī Māhātmya
summary: A 13-chapter, c. 700-verse glorification of the Goddess embedded in the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa, in which a supreme Goddess slays Madhu and Kaiṭabha, Mahiṣāsura and Śumbha–Niśumbha; Coburn calls it the 'crystallization' of the Goddess tradition.
details:
Structure (GRETIL MkP numbering): DM 1 = MkP 81 Madhu and Kaiṭabha; DM 2–4 = MkP 82–84 Mahiṣāsura (the Goddess formed from the gods' tejas 82.8–18, armed by them 82.19–30, riding a lion given by Himavat 82.29); DM 5–10 = MkP 85–90 Śumbha and Niśumbha (Ambikā/Kauśikī emerges from Pārvatī's body sheath 85.40–44; Kālī springs from her brow 87.5 and is named Cāmuṇḍā 87.26; Raktabīja 88); DM 11 = MkP 91 Nārāyaṇī-stuti; DM 12–13 = MkP 92–93 benefits and boons to Suratha and Samādhi.

A verse of DM 11 ('sarvamaṅgalamāṅgalye…', MkP 91.9 here) is quoted in the Dadhimatī-mātā inscription of 608 CE, a terminus ante quem for at least that hymn. In liturgical use it is the Durgāsaptaśatī / Caṇḍīpāṭha, whose 700-verse numbering differs from the Purāṇa's.

name: Matsya Purāṇa
summary: A Mahāpurāṇa presented as taught by Viṣṇu in fish form to Manu (1.10–2.19); it preserves a detailed list of the eighteen Purāṇas with verse counts and the five marks (53), the doctrine of ten manifestations caused by Bhṛgu's curse (47), and Satī's 108 tīrtha-names (13).
details:
Verified loci (Calcutta 1954 text on GRETIL): the fish identified as Janārdana/Vāsudeva (1.25–28; 2.17); the flood at the end of the Cākṣuṣa manvantara (2.14); twelve wars of gods and demons (47.41–45); ten manifestations of Viṣṇu due to Bhṛgu's curse — three divine and seven human (47.235–251); the eighteen Purāṇas with themes, verse counts and gifts (53.12–58), the upabhedas (53.60–63), the five marks (53.65) and the guṇa correlation (53.68–69); Satī's 108 names at tīrthas (13.26–53).

Rocher (1986) stresses that no Purāṇa can be dated as a whole: each is a layered, 'fluid' text transmitted in divergent manuscript versions, so any date applies only to a layer, a recension or a datable reference.

summary: Counted 'first of all Purāṇas' (ViP 3.6.20), the extant Brahma Purāṇa is largely a compilation of tīrtha material for Orissa (Puruṣottama/Puri, Koṇārka) and the Godāvarī, much of it borrowed from other Purāṇas and generally dated late.
details: Hazra held the extant text to be compiled no earlier than the 10th century; its description of Koṇārka suggests the Orissa chapters postdate the 13th-century temple (Wilson, Winternitz). Rocher (1986) stresses that no Purāṇa can be dated as a whole: each is a layered, 'fluid' text transmitted in divergent manuscript versions, so any date applies only to a layer, a recension or a datable reference.

name: Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa

name: Nārada Purāṇa
summary: A Vaiṣṇava Mahāpurāṇa (also Nāradīya; distinct from the Bṛhannāradīya Upapurāṇa) whose Pūrvabhāga contains a detailed synopsis (anukramaṇī) of all eighteen Purāṇas.
details: Its synopsis lists Vāyavīya in fourth place (NārP 1.92.26) and then describes each Purāṇa in turn (from 1.92). Hazra dates the related Bṛhannāradīya to the 9th century and places the Nāradīya after it. Rocher (1986) stresses that no Purāṇa can be dated as a whole: each is a layered, 'fluid' text transmitted in divergent manuscript versions, so any date applies only to a layer, a recension or a datable reference.

name: Bhaviṣya Purāṇa
summary: The 'Purāṇa of the future', a heterogeneous compilation with an early core on vows and Sun worship (shared with the Sāmba Purāṇa) and a Pratisargaparvan that 'prophesies' Mughal and even British-era history — accretions dated to the 18th–19th centuries.
details: Matsya 53.31–32 describes a Bhaviṣya taught by Brahmā to Manu concerning Āditya's greatness (14,500 verses). Hazra calls the extant work 'a loose collection of materials taken from various sources'; Hiltebeitel dates much of the Pratisargaparvan to the 19th century. Rocher (1986) stresses that no Purāṇa can be dated as a whole: each is a layered, 'fluid' text transmitted in divergent manuscript versions, so any date applies only to a layer, a recension or a datable reference.

name: Devī Bhāgavata Purāṇa
summary: A twelve-book Śākta Purāṇa that reworks the Bhāgavata model around the Goddess as supreme reality; Śāktas count it as the Mahāpurāṇa 'Bhāgavata', while most lists and scholars treat it as an Upapurāṇa.
details:
It retells the Devī Māhātmya battles (book 5), Satī's death and the seats of the Goddess (7.30), and contains the Devī Gītā (7.31–40, verified on GRETIL). Its partisans argue that the Matsya Purāṇa's description of 'the Bhāgavata' as beginning with the Gāyatrī and containing the slaying of Vṛtra (MatsP 53.20–21) fits the Devī Bhāgavata rather than the Śrīmad Bhāgavata.

Most scholars date it between the 9th and 14th centuries: Hazra to the 11th–12th, Pintchman 1000–1200, with parts of book 9 later (12th–15th).

name: Manusmṛti
summary: The most influential Dharmaśāstra, a verse treatise presented as Manu's (and Bhṛgu's) teaching; its first chapter gives a cosmogony and a yuga reckoning of 12,000 years for the four ages (1.68–73), the base of the Purāṇic scheme.
details: Manu 1.64–67 builds the time scale (nimeṣa → kāṣṭhā → kalā → muhūrta → day; a month is a day-night of the ancestors; a year a day-night of the gods); 1.68–71 gives Kṛta 4,000 years with sandhyā and sandhyāṃśa of 400 each, the others decreasing by a thousand and a hundred, totalling 12,000 — 'a yuga of the gods'; 1.72–73 a thousand such divine yugas make a day of Brahmā; 1.79 a manvantara is seventy-one of them. Manu does not itself multiply by 360; commentators and the Purāṇas read the 12,000 as divine years. The same verses occur in MBh (CE) 12.224.14–31.

name: Kālikā Purāṇa

details: Estimates for different sections range from the 7th to the 12th century (Rocher); several scholars favour the 10th–11th century. It is among the earliest texts devoted to Kāmākhyā.

name: Āryabhaṭīya
summary: Āryabhaṭa's astronomical treatise (499 CE), which states that he was 23 years old when 3,600 years of the Kali age had elapsed (3.10) — the basis of the later standard computation of the Kali epoch to 3102 BCE; it divides the mahāyuga into four equal quarters (3.10, cf. 1.5).
details: Verse 3.7 gives the scale: the solar (human) year ×30 = a year of the ancestors, ×12 = a divine year (i.e. 360 human years); 3.8 a mahāyuga is 12,000 divine years and a day of Brahmā 1,008 such yugas (not 1,000). The 'Thursday of the Bhārata' (1.5) marks the Kali epoch in his reckoning.

name: Viṣṇu
summary: A Vedic god of the three strides who in the epics and Purāṇas becomes, for Vaiṣṇavas, the supreme being who preserves the world and descends in avatāras; the Viṣṇu and Bhāgavata Purāṇas are his principal Purāṇic scriptures.
details: In the Ṛgveda Viṣṇu is a minor god celebrated for three strides (RV 1.154). By the late epic he is identified with Nārāyaṇa and Vāsudeva-Kṛṣṇa, and the Purāṇas make him the source of a series of descents whose number and membership vary by text (see the avatāra comparison). In the trimūrti scheme he preserves while Brahmā creates and Śiva destroys, though each sectarian Purāṇa subordinates the other two to its own god.

name: Śiva
summary: The great god of Śaiva traditions, identified, from the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad onward, with the Vedic Rudra; in the Purāṇas he is the ascetic and householder of Kailāsa, destroyer of Tripura and of Dakṣa's sacrifice, and, in the Liṅgodbhava, the infinite pillar of fire beyond Brahmā and Viṣṇu.

limits: An umbrella category.

name: Smārta tradition
summary: Brahmanical orthopraxy based on the smṛti (Dharmaśāstra, Purāṇa), associated with the worship of five deities (pañcāyatana: Viṣṇu, Śiva, Devī, Sūrya, Gaṇeśa) and, since the medieval period, with Advaita monasteries.
limits: Attribution of the pañcāyatana to Śaṅkara is traditional.

name: Early Bhāgavata (Vāsudeva) devotion
summary: The early devotional cult of Vāsudeva (and Saṅkarṣaṇa) whose adherents called themselves bhāgavata; the Heliodorus pillar's donor styles himself 'bhāgavata' (late 2nd c. BCE), and the tradition flows into later Vaiṣṇavism.
limits: The relation of this early cult to the later Bhāgavata Purāṇa is one of continuity of name and devotion, not of text.

name: Pāśupata Śaivism
summary: The earliest known Śaiva ascetic order, tracing itself to Lakulīśa (c. 2nd c. CE); its milieu shaped the Vāyu, Liṅga, Kūrma and the early Skandapurāṇa.
limits: Pāśupata self-descriptions and inscriptions (material domain) are the primary evidence.

name: Saura (Sun) worship
summary: Worship of Sūrya as supreme, prominent in western and northern India between the Gupta and early medieval periods, with Maga priests from 'Śākadvīpa'; textual charters are the Sāmba and parts of the Bhaviṣya and Brahma Purāṇas.
limits: An umbrella category.

name: Gāṇapatya
summary: Traditions that worship Gaṇeśa as supreme, crystallised in the Gaṇeśa and Mudgala Upapurāṇas (2nd millennium) and in Maharashtrian centres such as Morgaon and Chinchwad.
limits: An umbrella category.

name: The Kali age began in 3102 BCE
summary: The traditional Indian astronomical epoch of the Kali-yuga (midnight 17/18 February 3102 BCE, Ujjain, as computed in later siddhāntas), derived backwards from planetary models; Āryabhaṭa's 499 CE statement implies it, and the 634 CE Aihole inscription counts 3,735 years from the Bhārata war.
details: Āryabhaṭa (AB 3.10) was 23 when 3,600 years of Kali had passed, i.e. Kali 3600 = 499 CE, giving an epoch of 3102 BCE (astronomical year −3101). The Aihole inscription of Pulakeśin II (Śaka 556 = 634/635 CE) dates itself 3,735 years after the Bhārata war, consistent with equating the war with the Kali epoch. Fleet (1911) argued the era was an astronomers' construction of about the 5th–6th century; the Purāṇas place the onset of Kali at Kṛṣṇa's departure (ViP 4.24.27, 4.24.32; 5.38.8) without giving a CE equivalent.
limits: A traditional and astronomical epoch; it is not evidence for the date of the Bhārata war or of any narrated event.

name: The Devī Bhāgavata is the Mahāpurāṇa 'Bhāgavata'
summary: The Śākta position that the 'Bhāgavata' of the eighteen-lists is the Devī Bhāgavata, supported by the Matsya's description of the Bhāgavata as beginning with the Gāyatrī and containing the slaying of Vṛtra (MatsP 53.20–21); Vaiṣṇava tradition and most scholars hold it to be the Śrīmad Bhāgavata, with the Devī Bhāgavata an Upapurāṇa.

name: Vāsudeva was worshipped by self-styled bhāgavatas by the 2nd century BCE
summary: The scholarly conclusion, from the Heliodorus pillar (Besnagar), the Hāthībāḍā–Ghosuṇḍī and Mora well inscriptions and the coins of Agathocles, that a devotional cult of Vāsudeva (and Saṅkarṣaṇa) existed in the last centuries BCE, long before the Purāṇas.
limits: Establishes cult and devotion to Vāsudeva by the 2nd–1st c. BCE; not the historicity of Kṛṣṇa or the content of later Purāṇic theology.

name: Śiva was worshipped in iconic and liṅga form by the early centuries CE
summary: The conclusion, from the Gudimallam liṅga and Kuṣāṇa coinage (Wima Kadphises' deity with bull), that Śiva worship in liṅga and anthropomorphic form predates the Śaiva Purāṇas.
limits: Dates of the objects are debated (material domain); the evidence establishes worship, not Purāṇic narratives.

name: The Devī Māhātmya was in circulation by 608 CE
summary: A verse of the Devī Māhātmya's eleventh chapter is quoted in a dated inscription of 608 CE, giving a firm terminus ante quem for at least part of the text.
limits: Dates the hymn, not necessarily the whole of the Devī Māhātmya.

name: Āryabhaṭa
summary: Indian astronomer-mathematician (b. 476 CE) whose Āryabhaṭīya (499 CE) states his age in the Kali era and adopts a mahāyuga of four equal quarters.
limits: Historical person; his yuga model is an astronomical one, distinct from the Purāṇic 4:3:2:1 scheme.
